blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 5.1 Introduction

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This chapter is essentially a continuation of our study of
differentiation of functions in Class XI. We had learnt to
differentiate certain functions like polynomial functions and
trigonometric functions. In this chapter, we introduce the
very important concepts of continuity, differentiability and
relations between them. We will also learn differentiation
of inverse trigonometric functions. Further, we introduce a
new class of functions called exponential and logarithmic
functions. These functions lead to powerful techniques of
differentiation. We illustrate certain geometrically obvious
conditions through differential calculus. In the process, we
will learn some fundamental theorems in this area.

blocks.text: 5.2 Continuity

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We start the section with two informal examples to get a feel of continuity. Consider
the function

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$f(x) = \begin{cases} 1, \text{ if } x \le 0 \\ 2, \text{ if } x > 0 \end{cases}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This function is of course defined at every
point of the real line. Graph of this function is
given in the Fig 5.1. One can deduce from the
graph that the value of the function at $nearby$
points on $x$-axis remain $close$ to each other
except at $x = 0$. At the points near and to the
left of 0, i.e., at points like $-0.1, -0.01, -0.001$,
the value of the function is 1. At the points near
and to the right of 0, i.e., at points like 0.1, 0.01,

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
0.001, the value of the function is 2. Using the language of left and right hand limits, we
may say that the left (respectively right) hand limit of $f$ at 0 is 1 (respectively 2). In
particular the left and right hand limits do not coincide. We also observe that the value
of the function at $x = 0$ coincides with the left hand limit. Note that when we try to draw
the graph, we cannot draw it in one stroke, i.e., without lifting pen from the plane of the
paper, we can not draw the graph of this function. In fact, we need to lift the pen when
we come to 0 from left. This is one instance of function being not continuous at $x = 0$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, consider the function defined as

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$f(x) = \begin{cases} 1, \text{ if } x \neq 0 \\ 2, \text{ if } x = 0 \end{cases}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This function is also defined at every point. Left and the right hand limits at $x=0$
are both equal to 1. But the value of the
function at $x=0$ equals 2 which does not
coincide with the common value of the left
and right hand limits. Again, we note that we
cannot draw the graph of the function without
lifting the pen. This is yet another instance of
a function being not continuous at $x=0$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Naively, we may say that a function is
continuous at a fixed point if we can draw the
graph of the function $around$ that point without
lifting the pen from the plane of the paper.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Mathematically, it may be phrased precisely as follows:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Definition 1 Suppose $f$ is a real function on a subset of the real numbers and let $c$ be
a point in the domain of $f$. Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
More elaborately, if the left hand limit, right hand limit and the value of the function
at $x = c$ exist and equal to each other, then $f$ is said to be continuous at $x = c$. Recall that
if the right hand and left hand limits at $x = c$ coincide, then we say that the common
value is the limit of the function at $x = c$. Hence we may also rephrase the definition of
continuity as follows: a function is continuous at $x = c$ if the function is defined at
$x = c$ and if the value of the function at $x = c$ equals the limit of the function at
$x = c$. If $f$ is not continuous at $c$, we say $f$ is discontinuous at $c$ and $c$ is called a point
of discontinuity of $f$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 1 Check the continuity of the function $f$ given by $f(x) = 2x + 3$ at $x = 1$.

Solution First note that the function is defined at the given point $x = 1$ and its value is 5.
Then find the limit of the function at $x = 1$. Clearly

$$\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 1} (2x + 3) = 2(1) + 3 = 5$$

Thus $$\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = 5 = f(1)$$

Hence, $f$ is continuous at $x = 1$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 3 Discuss the continuity of the function $f$ given by $f(x) = |x|$ at $x = 0$.

Solution By definition

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} -x, \text{ if } x < 0 \\ x, \text{ if } x \ge 0 \end{cases}$$

Clearly the function is defined at $0$ and $f(0) = 0$. Left hand limit of $f$ at $0$ is

$$\lim_{x \to 0^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 0^-} (-x) = 0$$

Similarly, the right hand limit of $f$ at $0$ is

$$\lim_{x \to 0^+} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 0^+} x = 0$$

Thus, the left hand limit, right hand limit and the value of the function coincide at

$x = 0$. Hence, $f$ is continuous at $x = 0$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 5 Check the points where the constant function $f(x) = k$ is continuous.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution The function is defined at all real numbers and by definition, its value at any
real number equals $k$. Let $c$ be any real number. Then

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \lim_{x \to c} f(x) = \lim_{x \to c} k = k $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Since $f(c) = k = \lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ for any real number $c$, the function $f$ is continuous at
every real number.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 6 Prove that the identity function on real numbers given by $f(x) = x$ is
continuous at every real number.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution The function is clearly defined at every point and $f(c) = c$ for every real
number $c$. Also,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \lim_{x \to c} f(x) = \lim_{x \to c} x = c $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Thus, $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = c = f(c)$ and hence the function is continuous at every real number.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Having defined continuity of a function at a given point, now we make a natural
extension of this definition to discuss continuity of a function.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Definition 2 A real function $f$ is said to be continuous if it is continuous at every point
in the domain of $f$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This definition requires a bit of elaboration. Suppose $f$ is a function defined on a
closed interval $[a, b]$, then for $f$ to be continuous, it needs to be continuous at every
point in $[a, b]$ including the end points $a$ and $b$. Continuity of $f$ at $a$ means

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = f(a) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: and continuity of $f$ at $b$ means

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \lim_{x \to b^-} f(x) = f(b) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Observe that $\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x)$ and $\lim_{x \to b^+} f(x)$ do not make sense. As a consequence
of this definition, if $f$ is defined only at one point, it is continuous there, i.e., if the
domain of $f$ is a singleton, $f$ is a continuous function.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 7 Is the function defined by $f(x) = |x|$, a continuous function?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution We may rewrite $f$ as

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$f(x) = \begin{cases} -x, & \text{if } x < 0 \\ x, & \text{if } x \ge 0 \end{cases}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: By Example 3, we know that $f$ is continuous at $x = 0$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let $c$ be a real number such that $c < 0$. Then $f(c) = - c$. Also

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \lim_{x \to c} f(x) = \lim_{x \to c} (-x) = -c \qquad (\text{Why?}) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Since $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$, $f$ is continuous at all negative real numbers.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, let $c$ be a real number such that $c > 0$. Then $f(c) = c$. Also

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \lim_{x \to c} f(x) = \lim_{x \to c} x = c \qquad \text{(Why?)} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Since $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$, $f$ is continuous at all positive real numbers. Hence, $f$
is continuous at all points.

Example 10 Discuss the continuity of the function $f$ defined by

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} x+2, \text{if } x \leq 1 \\ x-2, \text{if } x > 1 \end{cases}$$

Solution The function $f$ is defined at all points of the real line.

Case 1 If $c < 1$, then $f(c) = c + 2$. Therefore, $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = \lim_{x \to c} (x+2) = c + 2$

Thus, $f$ is continuous at all real numbers less than 1.

Case 2 If $c > 1$, then $f(c) = c - 2$. Therefore,

$$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = \lim_{x \to c} (x-2) = c - 2 = f(c)$$

Thus, $f$ is continuous at all points $x > 1$.

$x = 1$ is

The right hand limit of $f$ at $x = 1$ is

$$\lim_{x \to 1^+} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 1^+} (x-2) = 1 - 2 = -1$$

Since the left and right hand limits of $f$ at $x = 1$

do not coincide, $f$ is not continuous at $x = 1$. Hence

$x = 1$ is the only point of discontinuity of $f$. The graph of the function is given in Fig 5.4.

By definition, $p$ is continuous at $c$. Since $c$ is any real number, $p$ is continuous at
every real number and hence $p$ is a continuous function.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 15 Find all the points of discontinuity of the greatest integer function defined
by $f(x) = [x]$, where $[x]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution First observe that $f$ is defined for all real numbers. Graph of the function is
given in Fig 5.8. From the graph it looks like that $f$ is discontinuous at every integral
point. Below we explore, if this is true.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig 5.8

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Case 1 Let $c$ be a real number which is not equal to any integer. It is evident from the
graph that for all real numbers $close$ to $c$ the value of the function is equal to $[c]$; i.e.,
$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = \lim_{x \to c} [x] = [c]$. Also $f(c) = [c]$ and hence the function is continuous at all real
numbers not equal to integers.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Case 2 Let $c$ be an integer. Then we can find a sufficiently small real number
$r > 0$ such that $[c - r] = c - 1$ whereas $[c + r] = c$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: This, in terms of limits mean that

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \lim_{x \to c^-} f(x) = c - 1, \quad \lim_{x \to c^+} f(x) = c $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Since these limits cannot be equal to each other for any $c$, the function is
discontinuous at every integral point.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: 5.2.1 Algebra of continuous functions

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the previous class, after having understood the concept of limits, we learnt some
algebra of limits. Analogously, now we will study some algebra of continuous functions.
Since continuity of a function at a point is entirely dictated by the limit of the function at
that point, it is reasonable to expect results analogous to the case of limits.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Theorem 1 Suppose $f$ and $g$ be two real functions continuous at a real number $c$.
Then

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(1) $f+g$ is continuous at $x=c$.
(2) $f-g$ is continuous at $x=c$.
(3) $f \cdot g$ is continuous at $x=c$.
(4) $\left(\frac{f}{g}\right)$ is continuous at $x=c$, (provided $g(c) \neq 0$).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Proof We are investigating continuity of $(f + g)$ at $x = c$. Clearly it is defined at
$x = c$. We have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$ \lim_{x \to c} (f + g)(x) = \lim_{x \to c} [f(x) + g(x)] \quad \text{(by definition of } f + g \text{)} $$

$$ = \lim_{x \to c} f(x) + \lim_{x \to c} g(x) \quad \text{(by the theorem on limits)} $$

$$ = f(c) + g(c) \quad \text{(as } f \text{ and } g \text{ are continuous)} $$

$$ = (f + g) (c) \quad \text{(by definition of } f + g \text{)} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Hence, $f + g$ is continuous at $x = c$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Proofs for the remaining parts are similar and left as an exercise to the reader.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Remarks

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(i) As a special case of (3) above, if $f$ is a constant function, i.e., $f(x) = \lambda$ for some
real number $\lambda$, then the function $(\lambda . g)$ defined by $(\lambda . g) (x) = \lambda . g(x)$ is also
continuous. In particular if $\lambda = -1$, the continuity of $f$ implies continuity of $-f$.
(ii) As a special case of (4) above, if $f$ is the constant function $f(x) = \lambda$, then the
function $\frac{\lambda}{g}$ defined by $\frac{\lambda}{g}(x) = \frac{\lambda}{g(x)}$ is also continuous wherever $g(x) \neq 0$. In
particular, the continuity of $g$ implies continuity of $\frac{1}{g}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The above theorem can be exploited to generate many continuous functions. They
also aid in deciding if certain functions are continuous or not. The following examples
illustrate this:

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 16 Prove that every rational function is continuous.

Solution Recall that every rational function $f$ is given by

$$f(x) = \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}, \ q(x) \neq 0$$

where $p$ and $q$ are polynomial functions. The domain of $f$ is all real numbers except
points at which $q$ is zero. Since polynomial functions are continuous (Example 14), $f$ is
continuous by (4) of Theorem 1.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 17 Discuss the continuity of sine function.

Solution To see this we use the following facts

$$\lim_{x \to 0} \sin x = 0$$

We have not proved it, but is intuitively clear from the graph of $\sin x$ near $0$.

Now, observe that $f(x) = \sin x$ is defined for every real number. Let $c$ be a real

number. Put $x = c + h$. If $x \to c$ we know that $h \to 0$. Therefore

$$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = \lim_{x \to c} \sin x$$

$$= \lim_{h \to 0} \sin(c + h)$$

$$= \lim_{h \to 0} [\sin c \cos h + \cos c \sin h]$$

$$= \lim_{h \to 0} [\sin c \cos h] + \lim_{h \to 0} [\cos c \sin h]$$

$$= \sin c + 0 = \sin c = f(c)$$

Thus $\lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = f(c)$ and hence $f$ is a continuous function.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Thus $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ and hence $f$ is a continuous function.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $Remark$ A similar proof may be given for the continuity of cosine function.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Example 18 Prove that the function defined by $f(x) = \tan x$ is a continuous function.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution The function $f(x) = \tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}$. This is defined for all real numbers such

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
that $\cos x \neq 0$, i.e., $x \neq (2n +1)\frac{\pi}{2}$. We have just proved that both sine and cosine
functions are continuous. Thus $\tan x$ being a quotient of two continuous functions is
continuous wherever it is defined.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
An interesting fact is the behaviour of continuous functions with respect to
composition of functions. Recall that if $f$ and $g$ are two real functions, then

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$(f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
is defined whenever the range of $g$ is a subset of domain of $f$. The following theorem
(stated without proof) captures the continuity of composite functions.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Theorem 2 Suppose $f$ and $g$ are real valued functions such that $(f \circ g)$ is defined at $c$.
If $g$ is continuous at $c$ and if $f$ is continuous at $g(c)$, then $(f \circ g)$ is continuous at $c$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: The following examples illustrate this theorem.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Example 19 Show that the function defined by $f(x) = \sin (x^2)$ is a continuous function.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution Observe that the function is defined for every real number. The function
$f$ may be thought of as a composition $g$ o $h$ of the two functions $g$ and $h$, where
$g(x) = \sin x$ and $h(x) = x^2$. Since both $g$ and $h$ are continuous functions, by Theorem 2,
it can be deduced that $f$ is a continuous function.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Example 20 Show that the function $f$ defined by

blocks.text: where $x$ is any real number, is a continuous function.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution Define $g$ by $g(x) = 1 - x + |x|$ and $h$ by $h(x) = |x|$ for all real $x$. Then

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 5.3. Differentiability

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Recall the following facts from previous class. We had defined the derivative of a real
function as follows:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Suppose $f$ is a real function and $c$ is a point in its domain. The derivative of $f$ at $c$ is
defined by

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(c+h) - f(c)}{h} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
provided this limit exists. Derivative of $f$ at $c$ is denoted by $f'(c)$ or $\left.\frac{d}{dx}(f(x))\right|_c$. The
function defined by

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
wherever the limit exists is defined to be the derivative of $f$. The derivative of $f$ is
denoted by $f'(x)$ or $\frac{d}{dx}(f(x))$ or if $y = f(x)$ by $\frac{dy}{dx}$ or $y'$. The process of finding
derivative of a function is called differentiation. We also use the phrase $differentiate$
$f(x)$ $with$ $respect$ $to$ $x$ to mean $find$ $f'(x)$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: The following rules were established as a part of algebra of derivatives:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(1) $(u \pm v)' = u' \pm v'$
(2) $(uv)' = u'v + uv'$ (Leibnitz or product rule)

(3) $\left( \frac{u}{v} \right)' = \frac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}$, wherever $v \neq 0$ (Quotient rule).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: The following table gives a list of derivatives of certain standard functions:

blocks.label: Table-caption
blocks.text: Table 5.3

blocks.label: Table
blocks.text:
$f(x)$ $x^n$ $\sin x$ $\cos x$ $\tan x$
$f'(x)$ $nx^{n-1}$ $\cos x$ $-\sin x$ $\sec^2 x$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Whenever we defined derivative, we had put a caution $provided$ $the$ $limit$ $exists$.
Now the natural question is; what if it doesn't? The question is quite pertinent and so is
its answer. If $\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(c+h) - f(c)}{h}$ does not exist, we say that $f$ is not differentiable at $c$.
In other words, we say that a function $f$ is differentiable at a point $c$ in its domain if both
$\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(c+h) - f(c)}{h}$ and $\lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{f(c+h) - f(c)}{h}$ are finite and equal. A function is said
to be differentiable in an interval $[a, b]$ if it is differentiable at every point of $[a, b]$. As
in case of continuity, at the end points $a$ and $b$, we take the right hand limit and left hand
limit, which are nothing but left hand derivative and right hand derivative of the function
at $a$ and $b$ respectively. Similarly, a function is said to be differentiable in an interval
$(a, b)$ if it is differentiable at every point of $(a, b)$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Theorem 3 If a function $f$ is differentiable at a point $c$, then it is also continuous at that
point.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Proof Since $f$ is differentiable at $c$, we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} = f'(c) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: But for $x \neq c$, we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$f(x) - f(c) = \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} \cdot (x - c)$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore $\lim_{x \to c} [f(x) - f(c)] = \lim_{x \to c} \left[ \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} \cdot (x - c) \right]$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
or $\lim_{x \to c} [f(x)] - \lim_{x \to c} [f(c)] = \lim_{x \to c} \left[ \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} \right] \cdot \lim_{x \to c} [(x - c)]$
$= f'(c) \cdot 0 = 0$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Hence $f$ is continuous at $x = c$.

blocks.text: Corollary 1 Every differentiable function is continuous.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
To study derivative of composite functions, we start with an illustrative example. Say,
we want to find the derivative of $f$, where

blocks.text:
One way is to expand $(2x + 1)^3$ using binomial theorem and find the derivative as
a polynomial function as illustrated below.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, observe that $f(x) = (h \circ g) (x)$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: where $g(x) = 2x + 1$ and $h(x) = x^3$. Put $t = g(x) = 2x + 1$. Then $f(x) = h(t) = t^3$. Thus

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The advantage with such observation is that it simplifies the calculation in finding
the derivative of, say, $(2x + 1)^{100}$. We may formalise this observation in the following
theorem called the chain rule.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Theorem 4 (Chain Rule) Let $f$ be a real valued function which is a composite of two

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: functions $u$ and $v$; i.e., $f = v \text{ o } u$. Suppose $t = u(x)$ and if both $\frac{dt}{dx}$ and $\frac{dv}{dt}$ exist, we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{df}{dx} = \frac{dv}{dt} \cdot \frac{dt}{dx} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We skip the proof of this theorem. Chain rule may be extended as follows. Suppose
$f$ is a real valued function which is a composite of three functions $u$, $v$ and $w$; i.e.,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$f = (w \text{ o } u) \text{ o } v$. If $t = v(x)$ and $s = u(t)$, then

$$ \frac{df}{dx} = \frac{d(w \text{ o } u)}{dt} \cdot \frac{dt}{dx} = \frac{dw}{ds} \cdot \frac{ds}{dt} \cdot \frac{dt}{dx} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
provided all the derivatives in the statement exist. Reader is invited to formulate chain
rule for composite of more functions.

blocks.label: Equation

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{df}{dx} = \frac{dv}{dt} \cdot \frac{dt}{dx} = \cos t \cdot 2x $$

there is no doubt about the dependence of $y$ on $x$ in either of the cases. When a
relationship between $x$ and $y$ is expressed in a way that it is easy to solve for $y$ and
write $y = f(x)$, we say that $y$ is given as an explicit function of $x$. In the latter case it

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
is implicit that $y$ is a function of $x$ and we say that the relationship of the second type,
above, gives function $implicitly$. In this subsection, we learn to differentiate implicit
functions.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 22 Find $\frac{dy}{dx}$ if $x - y = \pi$.

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text:
Solution One way is to solve for $y$ and rewrite the above as
$$y = x - \pi$$
But then
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = 1$$
Alternatively, directly differentiating the relationship w.r.t., $x$, we have
$$\frac{d}{dx}(x - y) = \frac{d\pi}{dx}$$
Recall that $\frac{d\pi}{dx}$ means to differentiate the constant function taking value $\pi$
everywhere w.r.t., $x$. Thus
$$\frac{d}{dx}(x) - \frac{d}{dx}(y) = 0$$
which implies that
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dx}{dx} = 1$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 23 Find $\frac{dy}{dx}$, if $y + \sin y = \cos x$.


Solution We differentiate the relationship directly with respect to $x$, i.e.,


$$\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{d}{dx}(\sin y) = \frac{d}{dx}(\cos x)$$


which implies using chain rule


$$\frac{dy}{dx} + \cos y \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} = -\sin x$$


This gives $$\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{\sin x}{1 + \cos y}$$


where $$y \neq (2n + 1) \pi$$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 5.4 Exponential and Logarithmic Functions

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Till now we have learnt some aspects of different classes of functions like polynomial
functions, rational functions and trigonometric functions. In this section, we shall
learn about a new class of (related) functions called exponential functions and logarithmic
functions. It needs to be emphasized that many statements made in this section are
motivational and precise proofs of these are well beyond the scope of this text.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The Fig 5.9 gives a sketch of $y = f_1(x) = x, y = f_2(x) = x^2, y = f_3(x) = x^3$ and $y = f_4(x)$
$= x^4$. Observe that the curves get steeper as the power of $x$ increases. Steeper the
curve, faster is the rate of growth. What this means is that for a fixed increment in the
value of $x (> 1)$, the increment in the value of $y = f_n(x)$ increases as $n$ increases for $n$
$= 1, 2, 3, 4$. It is conceivable that such a statement is true for all positive values of $n$,

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
where $f_n(x) = x^n$. Essentially, this means
that the graph of $y = f_n(x)$ $leans$ more
towards the $y$-axis as $n$ increases. For
example, consider $f_{10}(x) = x^{10}$ and $f_{15}(x)$
$= x^{15}$. If $x$ increases from 1 to 2, $f_{10}$
increases from 1 to $2^{10}$ whereas $f_{15}$
increases from 1 to $2^{15}$. Thus, for the same
increment in $x, f_{15}$ grow faster than $f_{10}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Upshot of the above discussion is that
the growth of polynomial functions is
dependent on the degree of the polynomial
function – higher the degree, greater is
the growth. The next natural question is:
Is there a function which grows faster than any polynomial function. The answer is in
affirmative and an example of such a function is

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Our claim is that this function $f$ grows faster than $f_n(x) = x^n$ for any positive integer $n$.
For example, we can prove that $10^x$ grows faster than $f_{100}(x) = x^{100}$. For large values
of $x$ like $x = 10^3$, note that $f_{100}(x) = (10^3)^{100} = 10^{300}$ whereas $f(10^3) = 10^{10^3} = 10^{1000}$.
Clearly $f(x)$ is much greater than $f_{100}(x)$. It is not difficult to prove that for all
$x > 10^3, f(x) > f_{100}(x)$. But we will not attempt to give a proof of this here. Similarly, by
choosing large values of $x$, one can verify that $f(x)$ grows faster than $f_n(x)$ for any
positive integer $n$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Definition 3 The exponential function with positive base $b > 1$ is the function

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: The graph of $y = 10^x$ is given in the Fig 5.9.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
It is advised that the reader plots this graph for particular values of $b$ like 2, 3 and 4.
Following are some of the salient features of the exponential functions:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(1) Domain of the exponential function is $\mathbf{R}$, the set of all real numbers.
(2) Range of the exponential function is the set of all positive real numbers.
(3) The point $(0, 1)$ is always on the graph of the exponential function (this is a
restatement of the fact that $b^0 = 1$ for any real $b > 1$).
(4) Exponential function is ever increasing; i.e., as we move from left to right, the
graph rises above.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(5) For very large negative values of $x$, the exponential function is very close to 0. In
other words, in the second quadrant, the graph approaches $x$-axis (but never
meets it).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Exponential function with base 10 is called the *common exponential function*. In
the Appendix A.1.4 of Class XI, it was observed that the sum of the series

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
is a number between 2 and 3 and is denoted by $e$. Using this $e$ as the base we obtain an
extremely important exponential function $y = e^x$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: This is called natural exponential function.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
It would be interesting to know if the inverse of the exponential function exists and
has $nice$ interpretation. This search motivates the following definition.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Definition 4 Let $b > 1$ be a real number. Then we say logarithm of $a$ to base $b$ is $x$ if
$b^x = a$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Logarithm of $a$ to base $b$ is denoted by $\log_b a$. Thus $\log_b a = x$ if $b^x = a$. Let us
work with a few explicit examples to get a feel for this. We know $2^3 = 8$. In terms of
logarithms, we may rewrite this as $\log_2 8 = 3$. Similarly, $10^4 = 10000$ is equivalent to
saying $\log_{10} 10000 = 4$. Also, $625 = 5^4 = 25^2$ is equivalent to saying $\log_5 625 = 4$ or
$\log_{25} 625 = 2$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
On a slightly more mature note, fixing a base $b > 1$, we may look at logarithm as
a function from positive real numbers to all real numbers. This function, called the
$logarithmic$ $function$, is defined by

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$\log_b : \mathbf{R}^+ \rightarrow \mathbf{R}$
$x \rightarrow \log_b x = y \quad \text{if } b^y = x$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
As before if the base $b = 10$, we say it
is common logarithms and if $b = e$, then
we say it is natural logarithms. Often
natural logarithm is denoted by $ln$. In this
chapter, $log \ x$ denotes the logarithm
function to base $e$, i.e., $ln \ x$ will be written
as simply $\log x$. The Fig 5.10 gives the plots
of logarithm function to base 2, $e$ and 10.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig 5.10

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Some of the important observations
about the logarithm function to any base
$b > 1$ are listed below:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(1) We cannot make a meaningful definition of logarithm of non-positive numbers
and hence the domain of log function is $\mathbf{R}^{+}$.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text: (2) The range of log function is the set of all real numbers.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text: (3) The point $(1, 0)$ is always on the graph of the log function.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(4) The log function is ever increasing,
i.e., as we move from left to right
the graph rises above.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(5) For $x$ very near to zero, the value
of $\log x$ can be made lesser than
any given real number. In other
words in the fourth quadrant the
graph approaches $y$-axis (but
never meets it).

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig 5.11

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(6) Fig 5.11 gives the plot of $y = e^x$ and
$y = ln x$. It is of interest to observe
that the two curves are the mirror
images of each other reflected in the line $y = x$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Two properties of ‘log’ functions are proved below:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(1) There is a standard change of base rule to obtain $\log_a p$ in terms of $\log_b p$. Let
$\log_a p = \alpha$, $\log_b p = \beta$ and $\log_b a = \gamma$. This means $a^\alpha = p$, $b^\beta = p$ and $b^\gamma = a$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Substituting the third equation in the first one, we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$(b^\gamma)^\alpha = b^{\gamma\alpha} = p$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Using this in the second equation, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$b^\beta = p = b^{\gamma\alpha}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: which implies $\beta = \alpha \gamma$ or $\alpha = \frac{\beta}{\gamma}$. But then

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\log_a p = \frac{\log_b p}{\log_b a}$$

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(2) Another interesting property of the log function is its effect on products. Let
$\log_b pq = \alpha$. Then $b^\alpha = pq$. If $\log_b p = \beta$ and $\log_b q = \gamma$, then $b^\beta = p$ and $b^\gamma = q$.
But then $b^\alpha = pq = b^\beta b^\gamma = b^{\beta + \gamma}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: which implies $\alpha = \beta + \gamma$, i.e.,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\log_b pq = \log_b p + \log_b q$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
A particularly interesting and important consequence of this is when $p = q$. In
this case the above may be rewritten as

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \log_b p^2 = \log_b p + \log_b p = 2 \log p $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: An easy generalisation of this (left as an exercise!) is

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \log_b p^n = n \log p $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
for any positive integer $n$. In fact this is true for any real number $n$, but we will
not attempt to prove this. On the similar lines the reader is invited to verify

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \log_b \frac{x}{y} = \log_b x - \log_b y $$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 25 Is it true that $x = e^{\log x}$ for all real $x$?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution First, observe that the domain of log function is set of all positive real numbers.
So the above equation is not true for non-positive real numbers. Now, let $y = e^{\log x}$. If
$y > 0$, we may take logarithm which gives us $\log y = \log (e^{\log x}) = \log x$. $\log e = \log x$. Thus
$y = x$. Hence $x = e^{\log x}$ is true only for positive values of $x$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
One of the striking properties of the natural exponential function in differential
calculus is that it doesn’t change during the process of differentiation. This is captured
in the following theorem whose proof we skip.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Theorem 5*

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(1) The derivative of $e^x$ w.r.t., $x$ is $e^x$; i.e., $\frac{d}{dx}(e^x) = e^x$.


(2) The derivative of $\log x$ w.r.t., $x$ is $\frac{1}{x}$; i.e., $\frac{d}{dx}(\log x) = \frac{1}{x}$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 26 Differentiate the following w.r.t. $x$:
(i) $e^{-x}$ (ii) $\sin (\log x), x > 0$ (iii) $\cos^{-1} (e^x)$ (iv) $e^{\cos x}$

Solution

(i) Let $y = e^{-x}$. Using chain rule, we have

$$\frac{dy}{dx} = e^{-x} \cdot \frac{d}{dx} (-x) = - e^{-x}$$

(ii) Let $y = \sin (\log x)$. Using chain rule, we have

$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \cos (\log x) \cdot \frac{d}{dx} (\log x) = \frac{\cos (\log x)}{x}$$

blocks.label: Footnote
blocks.text: * Please see supplementary material on Page 222.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: (iii) Let $y = \cos^{-1} (e^x)$. Using chain rule, we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{-1}{\sqrt{1-(e^x)^2}} \cdot \frac{d}{dx}(e^x) = \frac{-e^x}{\sqrt{1-e^{2x}}} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: (iv) Let $y = e^{\cos x}$. Using chain rule, we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = e^{\cos x} \cdot (-\sin x) = -(\sin x) e^{\cos x} $$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 5.5. Logarithmic Differentiation

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In this section, we will learn to differentiate certain special class of functions given in
the form

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: By taking logarithm (to base $e$) the above may be rewritten as

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \log y = v(x) \log [u(x)] $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Using chain rule we may differentiate this to get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{1}{y} \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} = v(x) \cdot \frac{1}{u(x)} \cdot u'(x) + v'(x) \cdot \log [u(x)] $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: which implies that

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = y \left[ \frac{v(x)}{u(x)} \cdot u'(x) + v'(x) \cdot \log[u(x)] \right] $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The main point to be noted in this method is that $f(x)$ and $u(x)$ must always be
positive as otherwise their logarithms are not defined. This process of differentiation is
known as $logarithms$ $differentiation$ and is illustrated by the following examples:

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 27 Differentiate $\sqrt{\frac{(x-3)(x^2+4)}{3x^2+4x+5}}$ w.r.t. $x$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 27 Differentiate $\sqrt{\frac{(x-3)\left(x^{2}+4\right)}{3 x^{2}+4 x+5}}$ w.r.t. $x$.


Solution Let $y=\sqrt{\frac{(x-3)\left(x^{2}+4\right)}{\left(3 x^{2}+4 x+5\right)}}$


Taking logarithm on both sides, we have


$$\log y=\frac{1}{2}\left[\log (x-3)+\log \left(x^{2}+4\right)-\log \left(3 x^{2}+4 x+5\right)\right]$$


Now, differentiating both sides w.r.t. $x$, we get


$$\frac{1}{y} \cdot \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{1}{(x-3)}+\frac{2 x}{x^{2}+4}-\frac{6 x+4}{3 x^{2}+4 x+5}\right]$$


or


$$\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{y}{2}\left[\frac{1}{(x-3)}+\frac{2 x}{x^{2}+4}-\frac{6 x+4}{3 x^{2}+4 x+5}\right]$$


$$=\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{(x-3)\left(x^{2}+4\right)}{3 x^{2}+4 x+5}}\left[\frac{1}{(x-3)}+\frac{2 x}{x^{2}+4}-\frac{6 x+4}{3 x^{2}+4 x+5}\right]$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 28 Differentiate $a^x$ w.r.t. $x$, where $a$ is a positive constant.

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text:
Example 28 Differentiate $a^x$ w.r.t. $x$, where $a$ is a positive constant.

Solution Let $y = a^x$. Then
$$\log y = x \log a$$
Differentiating both sides w.r.t. $x$, we have
$$\frac{1}{y} \frac{dy}{dx} = \log a$$
or
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = y \log a$$
Thus
$$\frac{d}{dx}(a^x) = a^x \log a$$
Alternatively
$$\frac{d}{dx}(a^x) = \frac{d}{dx}(e^{x \log a}) = e^{x \log a} \frac{d}{dx}(x \log a)$$
$$= e^{x \log a} \cdot \log a = a^x \log a.$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 29 Differentiate $x^{\sin x}$, $x > 0$ w.r.t. $x$.

Solution Let $y = x^{\sin x}$. Taking logarithm on both sides, we have

$$\log y = \sin x \log x$$

Therefore $$\frac{1}{y} \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} = \sin x \frac{d}{dx} (\log x) + \log x \frac{d}{dx} (\sin x)$$

or $$\frac{1}{y} \frac{dy}{dx} = (\sin x) \frac{1}{x} + \log x \cos x$$

or $$\frac{dy}{dx} = y \left[ \frac{\sin x}{x} + \cos x \log x \right]$$

$$= x^{\sin x} \left[ \frac{\sin x}{x} + \cos x \log x \right]$$

$$= x^{\sin x - 1} \cdot \sin x + x^{\sin x} \cdot \cos x \log x$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 30 Find $\frac{dy}{dx}$, if $y^x + x^y + x^x = a^b$.


Solution Given that $y^x + x^y + x^x = a^b$.
Putting $u = y^x$, $v = x^y$ and $w = x^x$, we get $u + v + w = a^b$


Therefore $$\frac{du}{dx} + \frac{dv}{dx} + \frac{dw}{dx} = 0 \quad \dots \quad (1)$$


Now, $u = y^x$. Taking logarithm on both sides, we have


$$\log u = x \log y$$


Differentiating both sides w.r.t. $x$, we have


$$\frac{1}{u} \cdot \frac{du}{dx} = x \frac{d}{dx} (\log y) + \log y \frac{d}{dx}(x)$$


$$= x \frac{1}{y} \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} + \log y \cdot 1$$


So $$\frac{du}{dx} = u \left( \frac{x}{y} \frac{dy}{dx} + \log y \right) = y^x \left[ \frac{x}{y} \frac{dy}{dx} + \log y \right] \quad \dots \quad (2)$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Also $v = x^y$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Taking logarithm on both sides, we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \log v = y \log x $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Differentiating both sides w.r.t. $x$, we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{1}{v} \cdot \frac{dv}{dx} = y \frac{d}{dx} (\log x) + \log x \frac{dy}{dx} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$= y \cdot \frac{1}{x} + \log x \cdot \frac{dy}{dx}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So $$\frac{dv}{dx} = v \left[ \frac{y}{x} + \log x \frac{dy}{dx} \right]$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = x^y \left[ \frac{y}{x} + \log x \frac{dy}{dx} \right] \qquad \dots (3) $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Again $w = x^x$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Taking logarithm on both sides, we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \log w = x \log x. $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Differentiating both sides w.r.t. $x$, we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{1}{w} \cdot \frac{dw}{dx} = x \frac{d}{dx} (\log x) + \log x \cdot \frac{d}{dx} (x) $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$= x \cdot \frac{1}{x} + \log x \cdot 1$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$y^x \left( \frac{x}{y} \frac{dy}{dx} + \log y \right) + x^y \left( \frac{y}{x} + \log x \frac{dy}{dx} \right) + x^x (1 + \log x) = 0$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $$(x . y^{x-1} + x^y . \log x) \frac{dy}{dx} = -x^x (1 + \log x) - y . x^{y-1} - y^x \log y$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{-[y^x \log y + y \cdot x^{y-1} + x^x(1 + \log x)]}{x \cdot y^{x-1} + x^y \log x}$$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 5.6 Derivatives of Functions in Parametric Forms

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Sometimes the relation between two variables is neither explicit nor implicit, but some
link of a third variable with each of the two variables, separately, establishes a relation
between the first two variables. In such a situation, we say that the relation between

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
them is expressed via a third variable. The third variable is called the parameter. More
precisely, a relation expressed between two variables $x$ and $y$ in the form
$x = f(t), y = g(t)$ is said to be parametric form with $t$ as a parameter.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In order to find derivative of function in such form, we have by chain rule.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dy}{dt} = \frac{dy}{dx} \cdot \frac{dx}{dt} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\frac{dy}{dt}}{\frac{dx}{dt}} \left( \text{whenever } \frac{dx}{dt} \neq 0 \right)$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Thus $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{g'(t)}{f'(t)} \left( \text{as } \frac{dy}{dt} = g'(t) \text{ and } \frac{dx}{dt} = f'(t) \right) \text{[provided } f'(t) \neq 0 \text{]}$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 31 Find $\frac{dy}{dx}$, if $x = a \cos \theta$, $y = a \sin \theta$.


Solution Given that
$$x = a \cos \theta, y = a \sin \theta$$
Therefore $$\frac{dx}{d\theta} = - a \sin \theta, \frac{dy}{d\theta} = a \cos \theta$$
Hence $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\frac{dy}{d\theta}}{\frac{dx}{d\theta}} = \frac{a \cos \theta}{-a \sin \theta} = -\cot \theta$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 32 Find $\frac{dy}{dx}$, if $x = at^2$, $y = 2at$.

Solution Given that $x = at^2$, $y = 2at$

So $\frac{dx}{dt} = 2at$ and $\frac{dy}{dt} = 2a$

Therefore $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\frac{dy}{dt}}{\frac{dx}{dt}} = \frac{2a}{2at} = \frac{1}{t}$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 33 Find $\frac{dy}{dx}$, if $x = a (\theta + \sin \theta)$, $y = a (1 - \cos \theta)$.


Solution We have $\frac{dx}{d\theta} = a(1 + \cos \theta)$, $\frac{dy}{d\theta} = a (\sin \theta)$


Therefore $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\frac{dy}{d\theta}}{\frac{dx}{d\theta}} = \frac{a \sin \theta}{a(1 + \cos \theta)} = \tan \frac{\theta}{2}$$

without directly involving the main variables $x$ and $y$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 34 Find $\frac{dy}{dx}$, if $x^{\frac{2}{3}} + y^{\frac{2}{3}} = a^{\frac{2}{3}}$.

Solution Let $x = a \cos^3 \theta$, $y = a \sin^3 \theta$. Then

$$x^{\frac{2}{3}} + y^{\frac{2}{3}} = (a \cos^3 \theta)^{\frac{2}{3}} + (a \sin^3 \theta)^{\frac{2}{3}}$$

$$= a^{\frac{2}{3}} (\cos^2 \theta + (\sin^2 \theta)) = a^{\frac{2}{3}}$$

Hence, $x = a \cos^3 \theta$, $y = a \sin^3 \theta$ is parametric equation of $x^{\frac{2}{3}} + y^{\frac{2}{3}} = a^{\frac{2}{3}}$

Now $\frac{dx}{d\theta} = - 3a \cos^2 \theta \sin \theta$ and $\frac{dy}{d\theta} = 3a \sin^2 \theta \cos \theta$

Therefore $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\frac{dy}{d\theta}}{\frac{dx}{d\theta}} = \frac{3a \sin^2 \theta \cos \theta}{-3a \cos^2 \theta \sin \theta} = -\tan \theta = -\sqrt[3]{\frac{y}{x}}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let $y = f(x)$. Then

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = f'(x) \hfill ... (1) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If $f'(x)$ is differentiable, we may differentiate (1) again w.r.t. $x$. Then, the left hand


side becomes $\frac{d}{dx} \left( \frac{dy}{dx} \right)$ which is called the *second order derivative* of $y$ w.r.t. $x$ and


is denoted by $\frac{d^2 y}{dx^2}$. The second order derivative of $f(x)$ is denoted by $f''(x)$. It is also


denoted by $\text{D}^2 y$ or $y''$ or $y_2$ if $y = f(x)$. We remark that higher order derivatives may be
defined similarly.

Example 35 Find $\frac{d^2 y}{dx^2}$, if $y = x^3 + \tan x$.

Solution Given that $y = x^3 + \tan x$. Then

$$\frac{dy}{dx} = 3x^2 + \sec^2 x$$

Therefore $$\frac{d^2 y}{dx^2} = \frac{d}{dx} (3x^2 + \sec^2 x)$$

$$= 6x + 2 \sec x . \sec x \tan x = 6x + 2 \sec^2 x \tan x$$

Example 36 If $y = \text{A} \sin x + \text{B} \cos x$, then prove that $\frac{d^2 y}{dx^2} + y = 0$.

Solution We have

$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \text{A} \cos x - \text{B} \sin x$$

and

$$\frac{d^2 y}{dx^2} = \frac{d}{dx} (\text{A} \cos x - \text{B} \sin x)$$

$$= - \text{A} \sin x - \text{B} \cos x = - y$$

Hence

$$\frac{d^2 y}{dx^2} + y = 0$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 40 Differentiate the following w.r.t. $x$.

(i)  $\cos^{-1} (\sin x)$      (ii)  $\tan^{-1} \left( \frac{\sin x}{1 + \cos x} \right)$      (iii)  $\sin^{-1} \left( \frac{2^{x+1}}{1 + 4^x} \right)$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text:
(i) Let $f(x) = \cos^{-1}(\sin x)$. Observe that this function is defined for all real numbers.
We may rewrite this function as
$$f(x) = \cos^{-1}(\sin x)$$
$$= \cos^{-1}\left[\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)\right]$$
$$= \frac{\pi}{2} - x$$
Thus $f'(x) = -1$.
(ii) Let $f(x) = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\sin x}{1 + \cos x}\right)$. Observe that this function is defined for all real
numbers, where $\cos x \neq -1$; i.e., at all odd multiplies of $\pi$. We may rewrite this
function as
$$f(x) = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\sin x}{1 + \cos x}\right)$$
$$= \tan^{-1}\left[\frac{2 \sin\left(\frac{x}{2}\right) \cos\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)}{2 \cos^2 \frac{x}{2}}\right]$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = \tan^{-1} \left[ \tan \left( \frac{x}{2} \right) \right] = \frac{x}{2} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Observe that we could cancel $\cos \left( \frac{x}{2} \right)$ in both numerator and denominator as it


is not equal to zero. Thus $f'(x) = \frac{1}{2}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: (iii) Let $f(x) = \sin^{-1} \left( \frac{2^{x+1}}{1+4^x} \right)$. To find the domain of this function we need to find all

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $x$ such that $-1 \le \frac{2^{x+1}}{1+4^x} \le 1$. Since the quantity in the middle is always positive,

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
may rewrite this as $2 \leq \frac{1}{2^x} + 2^x$ which is true for all $x$. Hence the function
is defined at every real number. By putting $2^x = \tan \theta$, this function may be
rewritten as

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$f(x) = \sin^{-1} \left[ \frac{2^{x+1}}{1+4^x} \right]$$
$$= \sin^{-1} \left[ \frac{2^x \cdot 2}{1+(2^x)^2} \right]$$
$$= \sin^{-1} \left[ \frac{2 \tan \theta}{1+\tan^2 \theta} \right]$$
$$= \sin^{-1} [\sin 2\theta]$$
$$= 2\theta = 2 \tan^{-1} (2^x)$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Thus $f'(x) = 2 \cdot \frac{1}{1 + (2^x)^2} \cdot \frac{d}{dx} (2^x)$

$= \frac{2}{1 + 4^x} \cdot (2^x) \log 2$

$= \frac{2^{x+1} \log 2}{1 + 4^x}$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 41 Find $f'(x)$ if $f(x) = (\sin x)^{\sin x}$ for all $0 < x < \pi$.
Solution The function $y = (\sin x)^{\sin x}$ is defined for all positive real numbers. Taking
logarithms, we have
$$\log y = \log (\sin x)^{\sin x} = \sin x \log (\sin x)$$
Then
$$\frac{1}{y} \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{d}{dx} (\sin x \log (\sin x))$$
$$= \cos x \log (\sin x) + \sin x \cdot \frac{1}{\sin x} \cdot \frac{d}{dx} (\sin x)$$
$$= \cos x \log (\sin x) + \cos x$$
$$= (1 + \log (\sin x)) \cos x$$
Thus $$\frac{dy}{dx} = y((1 + \log (\sin x)) \cos x) = (1 + \log (\sin x)) (\sin x)^{\sin x} \cos x$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 42 For a positive constant $a$ find $\frac{dy}{dx}$, where


$$y = a^{t+\frac{1}{t}}, \text{ and } x = \left( t + \frac{1}{t} \right)^a$$


Solution Observe that both $y$ and $x$ are defined for all real $t \neq 0$. Clearly


$$\frac{dy}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt} \left( a^{t+\frac{1}{t}} \right) = a^{t+\frac{1}{t}} \frac{d}{dt} \left( t + \frac{1}{t} \right) \cdot \log a$$


$$= a^{t+\frac{1}{t}} \left( 1 - \frac{1}{t^2} \right) \log a$$


Similarly $$\frac{dx}{dt} = a \left[ t + \frac{1}{t} \right]^{a-1} \cdot \frac{d}{dt} \left( t + \frac{1}{t} \right)$$


$$= a \left[ t + \frac{1}{t} \right]^{a-1} \cdot \left( 1 - \frac{1}{t^2} \right)$$


$$\frac{dx}{dt} \neq 0 \text{ only if } t \neq \pm 1. \text{ Thus for } t \neq \pm 1,$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$ \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\frac{dy}{dt}}{\frac{dx}{dt}} = \frac{a^{t+\frac{1}{t}} \left( 1 - \frac{1}{t^2} \right) \log a}{a \left[ t + \frac{1}{t} \right]^{a-1} \cdot \left( 1 - \frac{1}{t^2} \right)} $$


$$ = \frac{a^{t+\frac{1}{t}} \log a}{a \left( t + \frac{1}{t} \right)^{a-1}} $$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 43 Differentiate $\sin^2 x$ w.r.t. $e^{\cos x}$.

Solution Let $u(x) = \sin^2 x$ and $v(x) = e^{\cos x}$. We want to find $\frac{du}{dv} = \frac{du/dx}{dv/dx}$. Clearly

$$\frac{du}{dx} = 2 \sin x \cos x \text{ and } \frac{dv}{dx} = e^{\cos x} (-\sin x) = -(\sin x) e^{\cos x}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Thus $$\frac{du}{dv} = \frac{2 \sin x \cos x}{-\sin x e^{\cos x}} = -\frac{2 \cos x}{e^{\cos x}}$$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Summary

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
A real valued function is continuous at a point in its domain if the limit of the
function at that point equals the value of the function at that point. A function
is continuous if it is continuous on the whole of its domain.
Sum, difference, product and quotient of continuous functions are continuous.
i.e., if $f$ and $g$ are continuous functions, then
$(f \pm g) (x) = f(x) \pm g(x)$ is continuous.
$(f \cdot g) (x) = f(x) \cdot g(x)$ is continuous.

$$\left(\frac{f}{g}\right)(x) = \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} \text{ (wherever } g(x) \neq 0) \text{ is continuous.}$$

Every differentiable function is continuous, but the converse is not true.
Chain rule is rule to differentiate composites of functions. If $f = v \text{ o } u, t = u (x)$

and if both $\frac{dt}{dx}$ and $\frac{dv}{dt}$ exist then

$$\frac{df}{dx} = \frac{dv}{dt} \cdot \frac{dt}{dx}$$

Following are some of the standard derivatives (in appropriate domains):

$$\frac{d}{dx} (\sin^{-1} x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}} \quad \frac{d}{dx} (\cos^{-1} x) = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}$$

$$\frac{d}{dx} (\tan^{-1} x) = \frac{1}{1 + x^2}$$

$$\frac{d}{dx} (e^x) = e^x \quad \frac{d}{dx} (\log x) = \frac{1}{x}$$

Logarithmic differentiation is a powerful technique to differentiate functions
of the form $f(x) = [u (x)]^{v(x)}$. Here both $f(x)$ and $u(x)$ need to be positive for
this technique to make sense.
